data.title: Do Personalized Skills Help Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Developer Interaction Traces
data.description: arXiv:2608.10319v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As human developers increasingly collaborate with large language model (LLM)-powered coding agents, adapting to individual developer preferences, potentially via agent skills, may offer way to reduce repeated guidance and improve collaboration efficiency. However, existing approaches primarily focus on building skills for each task rather for each human developer. In this work, we propose a framework that combines rule-based bootstrapping with LLM-based refinement to distill developer-specific skills from their interactions with coding agents. We further develop an interactive replay framework with an LLM-based developer simulator for evaluation. We conduct experiments on a collection of replayable real-world developer-agent interaction sessions. We find that overall, task-specific skills are the most effective; However, personalized skills become more effective when developer preferences are manifested with enough frequency, especially when developers work on tasks that are highly related. These findings provide empirical insights suggest that i) broadly transferable procedural knowledge can be more robust than developer-specific preference signals and ii) effective personalization requires mining from rich user preference signals.
data.author: Shuyan Huang, Kai Du, Andrew Lan
